hints: Combine it with $-\tan\theta$ over one denominator.
Recognise $1-\tan^2\theta=\cos2\theta/\cos^2\theta$ to obtain the required $\sec2\theta$ factor.
walkthrough:
Apply the double angle formula for tangent $\tan 2\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta}$ to the left-hand side:
$$\tan 2\theta - \tan\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} - \tan\theta$$

Use the Pythagorean identity $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ and the double angle identity $\cos 2\theta = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta}$ which gives $\sec 2\theta = \dfrac{1 + \tan^2\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta}$:
$$= \tan\theta \cdot \dfrac{1 + \tan^2\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} = \tan\theta\sec 2\theta$$
This matches the right-hand side, completing the proof.

hints: Apply the bounds $0$ and $\pi/6$ to both logarithmic terms.
Insert the exact cosine values and combine logarithms to reach the stated expression.
walkthrough:
Use the identity from part (i) to rewrite the integrand:
$$\int_0^{\pi/6} \tan\theta\sec 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \int_0^{\pi/6} (\tan 2\theta - \tan\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Subtract the lower limit evaluation from the upper limit evaluation:
$$\int_0^{\pi/6} \tan\theta\sec 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$
